# Exact residue-level mass expansion, including oblique caps

This is an arithmetic volume theorem. It does not construct an OC center,
does not permit summing overlapping residue-class outputs, and is not a
proof of the remaining numerical bound at an arithmetic minimum. The
proof below is self-contained. Independent audit is pending.

## 1. A finite-source midpoint expansion

Let d>=1 and let A be a finite union of compact convex d-dimensional
fibers, with all its integer bases in one residue class modulo an integer
m>=2. Write M for its mixed d-volume and a for its largest fiber volume.
Let T be the set of averages of m points of A, chosen independently as
points of the set (not randomly). Every T-base is integral. Then

    mu(T) >= m M-(m-1)a.                              (1)

The T-fibers may be nonconvex finite unions. For t>0 let P_t be the
bases whose A-fiber has volume greater than t. Whenever p_1,...,p_m
belong to P_t, ordinary Brunn--Minkowski puts a set of volume greater
than t in the T-fiber at their average. Distinct averages are counted
only once.

A nonempty finite set P in a real vector space satisfies

    |P+...+P| >= m(|P|-1)+1.                          (2)

To prove this, choose a linear functional taking distinct values on P,
and list P as p_1,...,p_N in its increasing order. For j=0,...,m-1,
the successive lists

    (m-j-1)p_1+j p_N+p_i,       i=1,...,N,

are strictly increasing under that functional, except that the last
point of one list equals the first point of the next. They exhibit
m(N-1)+1 distinct members of the m-fold sum. For N=1 this also holds.

The layer-cake formula and (2) now give

    mu(T) >= integral_0^a [m |P_t|-(m-1)] dt
           =m M-(m-1)a.

If M=0 the assertion is immediate. No full-dimensionality of the
individual zero-volume fibers is needed; positive thresholds omit them.
For d=0 the analogous statement is just (2), with no root powers.

If A is contained in an actual convex body E, then T is contained in E.
In particular E=C intersect H can be any closed ambient cap, including
an oblique cap or a vertical cap with mass on its boundary. Thus (1)
gives a valid lower bound for mu(C intersect H) from any one residue
class of that same cap.

## 2. A lattice-polytope dilation bound, with proof

Let Q be a nonempty lattice polytope of affine dimension s and let
N=|Q intersect Z^n|. For every positive integer m,

    |m Q intersect Z^n|
       >= B_m(s,N)
        := binom(m+s,s)+(N-s-1)binom(m+s-1,s).        (3)

For s=0, N=1 and the right side is one. For s>=1 we work in the
saturated lattice of the affine hull after translating by an integer
vertex. This reduces to a full-dimensional lattice polytope in Z^s;
translation and the dilation translation m times that vertex preserve
the counts in (3).

Here are the generating-function details needed for (3). Triangulate Q
into full-dimensional simplices with integer vertices and common faces.
Such a triangulation can be obtained by ordering its vertices and pulling
the first vertex: recursively triangulate the facets not containing it
and cone to that vertex, using the induced vertex order on all faces.
Induction on face dimension makes the induced subdivisions agree.

The cones over these simplices, generated by (v,1) for their vertices,
triangulate the cone over Q in R^(s+1). Choose a vector xi in the interior
of the whole cone which lies in none of the finitely many linear spans
of cone facets. Assign a point w of the closed whole cone to the unique
simplex cone whose interior contains w+epsilon xi for every sufficiently
small epsilon>0. This is well defined: a boundary point moves inside the
whole cone, and at any cone facet through w the nonzero sign of xi
resolves which side is entered. The resulting half-open simplex cones
partition the closed cone, including its origin.

In one simplicial cone write w=sum_i lambda_i(v_i,1). Each coordinate
condition is either lambda_i>=0 or lambda_i>0. Let its fundamental
parallelepiped have lambda_i in [0,1) in the first case and (0,1] in the
second. Every integer point in that half-open cone is uniquely an integer
point of this bounded parallelepiped plus sum_i k_i(v_i,1), k_i>=0
integers. To see uniqueness, use the usual fractional part in a closed
coordinate and subtract ceil(lambda_i)-1 in an open coordinate. The
remainder is still an integer vector because all generators are integer.

Consequently its lattice generating function by the last coordinate is

    (sum_q t^(height(q))) / (1-t)^(s+1),

where q runs over its finitely many integer parallelepiped points. All
heights are nonnegative integers, at most s+1. Summing over the disjoint
half-open cones gives

    sum_(j>=0) |jQ intersect Z^s| t^j
            = (sum_l h_l t^l)/(1-t)^(s+1),          (4)

with h_l nonnegative integers. The coefficient at zero is one, so h_0=1.
The coefficient at one is N, so h_1=N-s-1. All remaining coefficients
in the numerator are nonnegative. Retaining just these first two terms
in (4), and taking the coefficient at t^m, proves (3). This argument
does not need the stronger usual assertion that the numerator degree
is at most s; permitting degree s+1 causes no problem for the bound.

## 3. The dimension-stratified cap inequality

Let E be a compact convex set in R^n times R^d, d>=1, with only finitely
many nonzero measured fibers. It need not have interior in the whole
ambient space. Fix a residue representative r in Z^n and m>=2. Put

    w_p=vol_d(E_p),
    A_t={p in r+m Z^n:w_p>t},
    N_t=|A_t|,   s_t=dim aff(A_t) when A_t is nonempty,
    a_r=max_(p in r+m Z^n) w_p.

Empty maxima are interpreted as zero. Then

    mu(E) >= integral_0^(a_r) B_m(s_t,N_t) dt.       (5)

All expressions are finite step functions of t; values at their finitely
many jumps do not affect the integral. If a_r=0 the right side is zero.

For a nonempty A_t define the lattice polytope

    Q_t=conv{(p-r)/m:p in A_t}.

It has exactly N_t lattice points. Indeed, if q is an integer point of
Q_t, then r+m q is a convex combination of bases in A_t. The corresponding
fiber contains their Minkowski combination. Brunn--Minkowski makes its
volume greater than t, so this base already belongs to A_t.

For every integer q in m Q_t, the integer base r+q is a convex combination
of the same original bases in A_t. The identical argument gives
w_(r+q)>t. Thus the total number of E-fibers of volume greater than t is
at least |m Q_t intersect Z^n|, which is at least B_m(s_t,N_t) by (3).
Integrating this count proves (5).

There is no loss from integer bases outside the affine hull of A_t:
they only add to the left side. Within that affine hull the saturated
lattice used in (3) counts precisely the ambient integer points there.
No arbitrary real affine map of the original mixed lattice is used.

For m=2 the integrand simplifies to

    B_2(s,N)=(s+1)N-s(s+1)/2.                       (6)

It is at least 2N-1 for N>=s+1: the difference is
(s-1)(N-(s+2)/2), nonnegative for s>=1; for s=0 both are one.
Consequently (5) strengthens

    mu(E) >= 2 sum_(p in r+2Z^n) w_p-a_r.           (7)

More generally (1) applied inside E always gives
mu(E)>=m sum_(p in r+mZ^n)w_p-(m-1)a_r.

Set E=C intersect H to obtain (5)-(7) for every closed ambient halfspace
H with all of its actual cap-fiber volumes. The proof does not discard
supporting fibers, and its use of positive d-volume thresholds is only
the layer-cake identity for that very same d-volume measure.

## 4. Sharp calibrations and the remaining limitation

For rank one let E=[0,m(N-1)] times K, where K is a d-dimensional body
of volume V. Restrict the source class to bases divisible by m. It has
N fibers, each of volume V. The whole source has m(N-1)+1 fibers. Thus
(1), (3), and (5) are all equalities. Additional integer coordinates can
be given width less than one, so this also has a full-dimensional convex
realization without creating additional integer bases.

For rank s let E=(m Delta_s) times K, with Delta_s the standard unimodular
simplex. In the all-zero class modulo m there are exactly the s+1 vertex
fibers, each of volume V. Here Q_t=Delta_s for 0<t<V, so (5) is equality:

    mu(E)=binom(m+s,s)V.

The lattice count is elementary: nonnegative integer coordinates with sum
at most m correspond, by adding a slack coordinate, to s+1 nonnegative
integers with sum m. Placing s separators among m+s positions gives the
binomial coefficient. In particular m=2 exactly recovers the source of
the largest-parity-mass depth obstruction.

The output sets constructed for different residue classes can overlap.
Their separate lower bounds in (5) may be maximized but cannot be added.
Also (5) is a statement about each already chosen cap. It supplies no
single point whose containing caps all have a prescribed amount of one
residue class. These two issues remain necessary for any use in OC.
